summary.name: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
summary.one_liner: SIP is a text-based application-layer signaling protocol for setting up, modifying, and ending voice, video, and messaging sessions, described on this Wikipedia page.
keywords: how do voip calls get set up
sip ua user agent client server
use_cases: Setting up and tearing down VoIP phone calls
Routing calls from a PBX to the PSTN via SIP trunking
Instant messaging and presence over SIP (SIMPLE)
Securing SIP signaling with TLS and media with SRTP
Connecting SIP-enabled cameras or audio-over-IP equipment
summary.what_it_does: The page describes SIP as a signaling protocol that initiates, maintains, modifies, and terminates multimedia sessions, using a text format similar to HTTP and SMTP. It explains the network elements involved, including user agents, proxy servers, redirect servers, registrars, session border controllers, and gateways. It lists SIP request methods (such as INVITE, REGISTER, BYE, MESSAGE) and response code classes. It also covers transport options (UDP, TCP, SCTP), TLS and SRTP encryption, and the NIST reference Java implementation.
notable: Text-based protocol modeled on HTTP, using SDP for media negotiation
Standardized by IETF in RFC 2543 (1999) and RFC 3261 (2002)
Adopted as a 3GPP signaling protocol in IMS and VoLTE
NIST provides a public-domain Java reference implementation
caveats: SIPS only secures the first hop; end-to-end encryption requires a direct connection
SDES key exchange sends keys over insecure SIP unless SIPS is used
